holidays.name: Pepper Pot Day
holidays.description: A day to enjoy Philadelphia Pepper Pot, a thick, peppery stew of tripe, vegetables and spices. Tripe soup isn't for everyone, so this is a good day to be brave with your spoon.
holidays.origin: Legend says that on December 29, 1777, cooks for George Washington's Continental Army served the soup to freezing troops at Valley Forge. Historians doubt the tale. The dish itself is older and has roots in West African and Caribbean cooking. Black women cooks and street vendors in Philadelphia helped make it famous.
holidays.funFact: The soup is nicknamed "the soup that won the war." The story says the cook made it from scraps, and the scraps may have been mostly tripe and peppercorns.

holidays.name: Still Need To Do Day
holidays.description: A gentle year-end nudge to look at your to-do list and finish what's left before the calendar flips. It's the perfect excuse to answer that email, return that borrowed casserole dish, or admit that a task will become next year's problem.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It fits neatly into the last few days of the year, when unfinished business is on everyone's mind.
holidays.funFact: Only two days remain after December 29, so the day doubles as a last call for New Year's resolutions you meant to start earlier.

holidays.name: International Cello Day
holidays.description: A celebration of the cello, the deep, warm-voiced string instrument that is often said to sound the most like the human voice. Cellists and fans mark the day with concerts, listening parties and a lot of Bach.
holidays.origin: The observance falls on the birthday of Pablo Casals, born December 29, 1876. He was a Catalan cellist and conductor who helped make the cello a major solo instrument.
holidays.funFact: Casals is credited with reviving Bach's Cello Suites as concert pieces. Before him, many musicians treated them as dry practice exercises.
